newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak cbank sees 96 real GDP growth of 6.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Slovak cbank sees 96 real GDP growth of 6.8 pct.

text.p: Slovak real GDP growth for 1996 should be 6.8 percent, the same as last year, central bank Governor Vladimir Masar said on Tuesday.

He added that the country's current account should finish the year with a $1.9-billion deficit, while the capital account, boosted by strong inflows of short-term funds, should end the year with a surplus of $2.1 billion.
"The NBS forecasts full year 1996 GDP growth at about 6.8 percent," Masar told a news conference.
Real GDP growth for the first three quarters of 1996, the latest official figures available, was 7.0 percent.
Masar added that some 45.3 percent of the capital account can be attributed to short-term capital (inflows).
"The central bank does not regard last year's monetary development as positive," he said.

"(This is) because of too rapid an expansion of domestic sources which negatively influenced the money supply but also the net foreign assets which were lower by eight billion crowns than originally planned," he added.
Masar also said that he expects the trade deficit for this year to account for less than five percent of the forecast GDP, though he did not give a crown figure for his 1997 trade deficit forecast.
The 1996 trade deficit rose to 64.5 billion crowns from 2.1 billion for 1995, and was 7.06 billion crowns for January 1997 alone.

But Masar said he expected the widening trend to reverse over the coming months. "The central bank expects the negative development of the trade deficit to reverse as a result of its strict measures aimed to curb growth of M2 and loan expansion."
Masar also said foreign exchange reserves covered a suitable amount of the country's imports, but that the NBS would act "promptly" to tap external sources if reserves start to show a negative trend.
He said the central bank's hard currency reserves totalled $3.5 billion at the end of February, up $0.2 billion from the beginning of this year, covering 3.3 months worth of imports.
"This development is favourable and the reserves are suitable, but we will be ready to act promptly and seek outstanding sources if the trend reverses," Masar said.
